edges.relationship: A call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ and ‘the significance of the sexes, of gender groups’, quoted by Joan Scott as an early relational use of gender (1975–76; Scott 1986)
edges.evidence_note: A reader’s explicit claim, read. Scott, ‘Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis’, AHR 91:5 (1986), p. 1054: those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men, that we should not be working only on the subjected sex any more than an historian of class can focus entirely on peasants. Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past.”’ (n. 4, citing Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s 1976 article is unread; her words are as Scott quotes them. Her own retrospect (1997, p. 16, read) describes the same programme: ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men in different times and places’. The Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘Her work brings gender to the fore’. A precursor statement taken up in Scott’s argument, not a claim that Davis founded gender history or shared Scott’s later theoretical position.

edges.relationship: Women and the relations of the sexes in early modern towns and festive life, and, with Jill Conway, a first Canadian course in women’s history (1971–75)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (Haskins Lecture, 1997, read in full): ‘In 1971, Jill and I organized the first course in women’s history in Canada, Society and the Sexes in Early Modern Europe and in America’ (p. 16, her claim); ‘City Women and Religious Change’ and ‘Women on Top’ show ‘this hope to build upon rather than abandon one form of history for another’ (p. 15); the field meant ‘simultaneously writing women into the historical record’, ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men’ and ‘re-evaluating the meaning of movements like the Reformation’ (p. 16). Hesse (AHA memorial, 2024, read in excerpts): ‘Her most transformative course was Society and the Sexes, a first in introducing the history of women’ into university curricula. Nussdorfer (SCS memorial, read) records two Sixteenth Century Society prizes in her name in early modern women’s, gender and sexuality studies. The 1970s essays (in Society and Culture, 1975) are unread; their content is as she describes it. edge_071 separately records the course as a route into Women on the Margins.
edges.map_label: Society and the Sexes; city women, 1971–75

edges.relationship: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with violence ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’ (1971–75)
edges.evidence_note: Her own text. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (Past & Present 59, 1973; pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91 read): violence is explained ‘in terms of the goals of their actions and in terms of the rôles and patterns of behaviour allowed by their culture. Religious violence is related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; it had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’ (p. 90); crowd violence has ‘some structure to it — here dramatic and ritual’ (p. 91). She sets this against Estèbe’s appeal to the ‘collective unconscious’ (p. 90). Her retrospect (1997, read): ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ began in 1969 from Van Gennep and Bakhtin (pp. 13–14); the title Society and Culture (1975) ‘seemed quite fresh and anthropological at the time’ (p. 15). Reception: Hunt’s New Cultural History (1989) makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ one of its models for cultural history in Desan’s chapter (publisher contents; chapter unread), and the graph’s earlier reading of Hunt’s introduction records her among its formative resources. Holberg committee (2010); Hesse (2024): ‘methodologically heterodox, incorporating anthropological and literary approaches’. Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and Davis’s rejoinder (Past & Present 67) are unread.

edges.relationship: Lyon’s printing workers, a journeymen’s organization and the religious crowd: urban social history that keeps conflict, interest and several social axes (1959–75)
edges.evidence_note: Her own texts. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973, p. 53, read) builds on the crowd history ‘of George Rudé, Eric Hobsbawm, E. P. Thompson, Charles Tilly, Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie and others’ and extends it to religious riot, which ‘has not received analytical attention’. Retrospect (1997, read): her 1959 dissertation found Lyon’s Protestants ‘drawn from all the social orders’, organized ‘around the axis of emotional-spiritual class’, and she prefers ‘the concept of multiple axes … as contrasted with my earlier two-dimensional Marxist model’ (p. 11); ‘A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France’ (1966) was ‘my commitment to classic social history’ (p. 12), with unease at the ‘evolutionary approach’ of Hobsbawm’s Primitive Rebels (p. 13); ‘Conflict was part of the picture, not just community’ (p. 15). Nussdorfer (SCS memorial, read): ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. The 1966 article is unread.
edges.map_label: Lyon’s menu peuple and the crowd, 1959–75

edges.relationship: Thompson’s moral economy of the crowd, acknowledged and applied to the legitimation of religious riot (1973)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgement, in period. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973, read): n. 6 on p. 53 lists ‘those works which have especially assisted the preparation of this paper’, including Thompson, ‘The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century’ (Past and Present, 1971). On p. 61: ‘E. P. Thompson has shown how in the eighteenth-century English food-riot, the crowd’s behaviour was legitimated by a widely held belief that it was acting in place of the government … Now we can deduce some of the same assumptions from the actions of the religious crowds of the mid-sixteenth century’ (n. 26, citing pp. 91–115). Rudé, Hobsbawm, Tilly and Le Roy Ladurie are named as well; Thompson is one resource among several. Their correspondence of 1970–72 is edited by Walsham (2017; opening extract only).
edges.map_label: Moral economy into the religious crowd, 1973

edges.relationship: Her study of French youth abbeys and charivaris used by Thompson as ‘une étude importante’ in his essay on English rough music (1971–72)
edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s own text, read in excerpts. ‘« Rough Music » : le charivari anglais’, Annales ESC 27 (1972), in the 2020 Socio-anthropologie reprint (paragraph numbers; no Annales pages): ‘Dans une étude importante, Natalie Davis a examiné certains aspects du charivari en France au xvie siècle’ (¶36); he uses her findings on the kinds of charivari and the ‘quasi-institutionalised’ role of youth abbeys, citing ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ (Past and Present 50, 1971, pp. 41–75; n. 40), with further uses at nn. 51 and 59. He reads her as following Lévi-Strauss on ‘la masse de jeunes disponibles’ (¶48), which is his characterisation. Walsham (2017; opening extract read) calls the two essays ‘classics of twentieth-century historical writing’ and edits their letters of 1970–72 (unread). Hunt’s volume (1989) pairs them as a model for cultural history (Desan; chapter unread).

edges.relationship: Van Gennep’s folklore and Douglas on pollution and boundaries, then Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz, read for questions tested on sixteenth-century evidence (1969–1980s)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements, in period and in retrospect. 1973 (read): ‘For the theory in this paragraph, I have found helpful Mary Douglas’s remarks on the relation between pollution fears and concern for social boundaries (Purity and Danger … ch. 7)’ (p. 61, n. 25); Van Gennep’s Manuel de folklore français on the dead (p. 57, n. 17). 1997 (read in full): she found Van Gennep’s Manuel, but her essay ‘used only historical evidence’ and, ‘in contrast with the static unchanging portrait of ceremonial and customary life presented in Van Gennep’, ‘pointed to shifts’ (p. 14); ‘I went on to read in anthropology and folklore: E.E. Evans-Pritchard, Victor Turner, Clifford Geertz, Sidney Mintz, and many others … I read eclectically, indifferent to conflicts within anthropology, for I was not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (p. 14); ‘One term I co-taught a course with Clifford Geertz’ (p. 19); the Martin Guerre project ‘grew out of the practice of anthropological history’ (p. 17). Finlay (1988, p. 554, read) attributes the book’s ‘inventive aspects’ to ‘anthropology, ethnography, and literary criticism’. No single anthropologist is credited as the source, and no specifically Geertzian method is established.

edges.relationship: The Return of Martin Guerre: a village imposture reconstructed from legal, notarial and printed sources as conjectural ‘ethnography’, reached ‘via film’ (1982–83)
edges.evidence_note: Her own account (1997, p. 19, read): ‘Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie and Carlo Ginzburg came to write their splendid microhistories … as an expansion of their prose. I came to microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’; making a film ‘could be an approximation of the ethnographic experience’ (p. 18). Her method (‘On the Lame’, 1988, pp. 574–575, read): Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers, set in ‘concentric circles of research’ through village and criminal archives; ‘I worked as a detective … establishing a conjectural argument that made the best sense, the most plausible sense, of sixteenth-century evidence’, citing Collingwood and Ginzburg’s ‘Clues’ (History Workshop 9, 1980; n. 11). Reception: Finlay (1988, p. 553, read) places the book with Le Roy Ladurie’s and Ginzburg’s legal-record reconstructions: ‘Even within this select company … exceptional’; he quotes Le Roy Ladurie (New York Review of Books, 1983) calling it a ‘major work of historical reconstruction’ (p. 554; mediated). Holberg committee (2010): it ‘demonstrated to a broader public how an individual event in early modern France could illuminate overall mentalities’. The book is unread; the French edition (1982) appeared with the film.

edges.relationship: Finlay charges an ‘excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’ in her Bertrande de Rols; Davis answers that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question’ the book posed (1988)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Robert Finlay’s intervention in the debate over evidence in microhistory (micro/reconstruction_invention), not a verdict of the field. Finlay, AHR 93:3 (1988), 553–571, read in full: ‘Davis fails to show that her view of women in peasant society is relevant to the case she is examining’ (p. 557); ‘self-fashioning’ ‘is merely imposed on the historical record as an ingenious assertion’ (p. 564); ‘If historical records can be bypassed so thoroughly in the service of an inventive blend of intuition and assertion, it is difficult to see what distinguishes the writing of history from that of fiction’ (p. 569); ‘speculation, whether founded on intuition or on concepts drawn from anthropology and literary criticism, is supposed to give way before the sovereignty of the sources … Davis has permitted an excess of invention’ (p. 571). He praises ‘its eloquent portrait of peasant life … its emphasis on the central role of women’ (p. 569). Davis, ‘On the Lame’, AHR 93:3 (1988), 572–603, read in part: the question ‘is precisely the question I hoped readers would ask and reflect on’; she would have preferred a critique ‘more subject to “the sovereignty of sources” to which it claims loyalty’ (p. 572); ‘he plays Savonarola to my Montaigne. Fortunately, historical practice can profit from each stance’ (p. 574); ‘proto-feminist’ is ‘a careless reporting of my text’ (p. 584). The group endpoint locates Finlay’s critique within the debate over microhistorical reconstruction; it does not assign him membership in a school. Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian edition, cited by Finlay (p. 569 n. 71), is unread.

edges.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
edges.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.
edges.map_label: Charivari narrative; Fiction in the Archives, 1979–87

edges.relationship: Bloch’s Strange Defeat and Feudal Society as formative reading in her turn from the history of ideas to social history; Bloch and Power as the twentieth-century historians of her AHA address (1940s–1987)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read in full): ‘Before I graduated, I also read Marc Bloch’s Strange Defeat and learned that an historian can be a hero’ (p. 5); ‘I had been reading Marc Bloch’s Feudal Society, and was all ready when W. K. Jordan urged me take Ket’s Rebellion’ as her graduate work shifted ‘from the history of ideas to social history’ (p. 7); arriving in Lyon in 1952, ‘I rushed around Lyon … to find a monument to Marc Bloch’ (p. 8). Her AHA presidential address (1987; read in part through tool excerpts) considers ‘history’s two bodies’ through five historians, Bloch and Eileen Power among them, and per the tool’s summary ends on Bloch’s 1942 letter. An acknowledged formative reading recorded in retrospect; it does not make her an Annales historian: she wrote that its histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model for what I wanted to do’ (p. 13).

edges.relationship: Decentred comparison: European women’s lives set beside colonial domination and non-European respondents (1995), a Muslim traveller between worlds (2006), and a programme of ‘decentering history’ (2010)
edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read): Women on the Margins was to ‘expand the single microhistory into a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); she asked about ‘the uninvited French intrusion into the American woodlands’ and Merian’s ‘African and Indian slaves’ (p. 22), introduced ‘non-European women … not just as silent objects … but as active respondents’ (p. 22), and felt ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’, with a new project on ‘cultural mixture’ along ‘the caravan routes of North Africa’ (p. 23). The conclusion of Women on the Margins (davis_margins_primary, earlier reading) shows marginality coexisting with colonial domination. Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history, exploring cultural, geographical and religious interchange’; Women on the Margins and Trickster Travels explore ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’. ‘Decentering History’ (Holberg Symposium, 2010; abstract only) moves ‘beyond a focus on Europe or the West’. Hesse (2024): ‘there were no dark parts of the globe’. Trickster Travels (2006) and the 2011 article are unread. Subrahmanyam’s mediated link from Kafadar to Davis (1997) stays on edge_641.

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §8): AHA web text read in part through the WebFetch tool (three passes), which returns only short exact quotations; the AHA site refuses plain HTTP clients. Quoted: the header (‘A paper read at the annual meeting of the American Historical Association, December 28, 1987’); ‘I want to consider how historians have conceptualized the body of historical knowledge’; ‘Eileen Power was one of the creators of a new kind of social and economic history in England’; the main text says ‘only one female historian contributed an essay to it [the Annales] in the seventeen years of its existence’, and note 65 then discusses Thérèse Sclafert (‘has an article in the first volume (1929) of the Annales’) and Lucie Varga (‘a refugee from Austria’, who ‘contributed an ethnographic study of an Austrian valley’), calling Varga ‘the only other woman writing for the Annales’. edge_755.evidence_note: 1.119 assessment, superseded in revision 1.143: ‘Davis connects three contrasting lives with religious, social and colonial settings. Description supports the proposed comparative-biography scope; body-text verification remains outstanding.’ Revision 1.143: the body text is read for this claim. The graph’s primary selection (davis_margins_primary: prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216, acknowledgments pp. 340–344; read 2026-09-12) shows an explicitly imagined prologue, not testimony, and a conclusion that compares the three women while keeping religious difference and colonial domination in view. text_revisions.old: Uses contrasting seventeenth-century lives to investigate religion, writing and relations of power across Europe and its colonial outposts. Women on the Margins makes individual lives a route into broader historical questions.
text_revisions.new: A historian of sixteenth-century France whose work moved from the social history of Lyon’s printing workers to ritual, gender, storytelling and lives that crossed religious and colonial borders. By her own account (1997) she ‘combined archival work with the study of printed texts of multiple genres’, and Laurie Nussdorfer’s memorial calls her ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. In ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973) she argued that religious riot drew on ‘a store of punitive or purificatory traditions’ and had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’, so that such violence was ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; she explicitly distinguished explaining the ritual structure of violence from granting a right to commit it: ‘the rites of violence are not the rights of violence in any absolute sense’. She acknowledged the crowd histories of Rudé, Hobsbawm, Thompson and Tilly and applied Thompson’s account of the food riot’s legitimation to the religious crowd. By her own account she came to ritual through Van Gennep’s folklore and read Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically … not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (1997); Thompson, for his part, called her charivari essay ‘une étude importante’ (1972). Joan Scott (1986) quoted her call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ as an early relational use of gender, and with Jill Conway she taught in 1971 what she called ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’. In 1997 she said she came to microhistory, ‘or what I called ethnography’, through the film of Martin Guerre, on whose script she worked; her book followed in French (1982) and English (1983). Robert Finlay (1988) charged that she had ‘permitted an excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’; she answered that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question I hoped readers would ask’. In her 1997 retrospect she described the ‘fiction’ of Fiction in the Archives (1987) as ‘the crafting element’, not falsification, and Women on the Margins (1995) as ‘a decentered comparison’ of three lives, whose conclusion keeps religious difference and colonial domination in view. The Holberg committee (2010) described The Gift (2000) as illuminating ‘the intricate forms of pre-market exchange and reciprocity’, Slaves on Screen (2000) as dealing with ‘the alteration of historical material in contemporary film’ and Trickster Travels (2006), with Women on the Margins, as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; it saw her uniqueness in ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history’.
text_revisions.reason: Whole-field rewrite (evidence-davis.md §11.2): the 1.119 description covered only Women on the Margins.

text_revisions.new: Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023); dissertation on Lyon’s Protestants and printing workers (1959); “A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France” (Economic History Review, 1966); “The Reasons of Misrule: Youth Groups and Charivaris in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1971); “The Rites of Violence: Religious Riot in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1973; reprinted in Society and Culture in Early Modern France, 1975); “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (Feminist Studies, 1976; quoted by Scott, 1986); Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1982; the catalogue record also credits Jean-Claude Carrière and Daniel Vigne, scenarist and director of the 1982 film on whose script she worked) and The Return of Martin Guerre (Harvard, 1983); “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987; AHR 1988); Fiction in the Archives: Pardon Tales and Their Tellers in Sixteenth-Century France (1987); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988, reply to Finlay); Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995); A Life of Learning (Haskins Lecture, 1997); Slaves on Screen: Film and Historical Vision (2000); The Gift in Sixteenth-Century France (2000); Trickster Travels: A Sixteenth-Century Muslim between Worlds (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium, 2010); later titles named in Nussdorfer’s memorial (unread): Leo Africanus Discovers Comedy: Theatre and Poetry Across the Mediterranean (2021) and Listening to the Languages of the People: Lazare Sainéan on Romanian, Yiddish and French (2022). Readers and critics: E. P. Thompson (1972); Lawrence Stone (1979); Joan Scott (1986); Robert Finlay (1988); Lynn Hunt, ed., with Suzanne Desan’s chapter (1989); Judith Jackson Fossett (2001); Holberg Prize committee (2010); Alexandra Walsham (2017); Laurie Nussdorfer (2023); Carla Hesse (2024).

text_revisions.old: Comparative biography provides a connection beyond gender history. This entry is supported by a newly checked book description; its methodological interpretation still needs a fresh body-text check. Other career contributions remain in the preserved contexts.
text_revisions.new: Read for revision 1.143: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91; her Haskins Lecture, A Life of Learning (1997), in full, cited as her later account of her course, not as evidence of what the earlier works say; ‘On the Lame’ (1988), pp. 572, 574–576, 584, 587, 600 and 602–603; Finlay’s critique (1988) in full; Stone (1979), pp. 3 and 18; Scott (1986), p. 1054; and, earlier, the prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments of Women on the Margins. Thompson’s ‘Rough Music’ (1972, by paragraph in a 2020 reprint), her AHA address (1987) and the AHA memorial (2024) are read only in short excerpts. The Return of Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels and the 2021–22 books are unread: they supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations only, given in her own retrospect or in named readers’ words (the Holberg committee, Fossett, Finlay, Nussdorfer). Also unread: ‘Women’s History in Transition’ (1976; her words as Scott quotes them), Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and her rejoinder, Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian Martin Guerre, Desan’s 1989 chapter and the Davis–Thompson letters (Walsham 2017; opening only). She is not presented as the founder of microhistory, cultural history or gender history: by her own account Le Roy Ladurie and Ginzburg reached microhistory by other routes, Scott quotes her as one relational voice among others, and anthropology supplied questions tested on ‘only historical evidence’. Finlay’s charge of invention and her reply are both kept, as is Fossett’s criticism (2001) that Slaves on Screen ‘raises more questions than it answers’. Not to be confused with J. C. Davis (the Ranter debate) or Donald F. Davis (Canadian urban history).

text_revisions.old: The Return of Martin Guerre reconstructs a sixteenth-century village imposture case and is a standard example of microhistory in English. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.
text_revisions.new: The Return of Martin Guerre (French 1982, the year of the film; English 1983) treats a village imposture. In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) she described her reconstruction from Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers as a conjectural argument, and in 1997 she called her route ‘microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’. Finlay’s 1988 critique of its ‘invention’ and her reply are both recorded. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.

strand.title: Reconstruction, invention and the sovereignty of sources
strand.focus: In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) Davis described her reconstruction of a village imposture from legal, notarial and printed records as conjectural, citing Ginzburg’s evidential paradigm; Finlay contests where reconstruction becomes invention, and Davis replies that the boundary was the book’s question. Both positions are recorded; neither settles the method.
strand.works: The Return of Martin Guerre (1982–83); Finlay and Davis, AHR Forum (1988)

strand.title: Early modern women, the sexes and the history curriculum
strand.focus: Teaching and essays put women, and the relations between the sexes, into early modern European history. Davis calls the 1971 course the first in women’s history in Canada and Hesse a first in the curriculum; neither is a field origin.
strand.works: Society and the Sexes (course, 1971); “City Women and Religious Change” and “Women on Top” (in Society and Culture, 1975)
